deep.reconstruction:
The page has four unrelated jottings. The last one continues on p.180.

(1) 'Transformation des Ebnen' (conformal maps of the plane). Put t = x+iy and T = X+iY. Gauss asks for analytic maps t -> T that carry the circle |t| = a onto itself. His answer is
T = t*exp(i*(f(t/a) + f'(a/t))),
where f is arbitrary and f' is its 'Adjuncte', i.e. the function with conjugated coefficients: f'(s) = conj(f(conj s)).
Verification (mine): on |t| = a we have a/t = conj(t)/a, so f'(a/t) = conj(f(t/a)). The exponent is therefore i*2*Re f(t/a), which is purely imaginary, so |T| = |t| = a.
Conversely (mine): any T analytic and non-vanishing near the circle, mapping it to itself with degree 1, has log(T/t) single-valued in an annulus and purely imaginary on the circle. Its Laurent series then has exactly this symmetric form. Möbius automorphisms of the disc are included locally, since T/t has winding number 0 on the circle. So the formula is a local general solution, essentially the reflection principle in Laurent-series form.

(2) Minimal surfaces. Let z be the height of a minimal surface z(x,y) over a point p of the projection plane. Map that plane to a second plane (by a 'Darstellung', presumably a conformal map as in (1)). At the image point erect a perpendicular of length z. Gauss asserts the new graph is again a minimal surface. See errors: this holds only for similarities.

(3) 'Theorem aus der Sphaerologie'. Setting: a spherical quadrilateral ABCD with right angles at A, B, C (a spherical Lambert quadrilateral, so D > 90°).
- Construction: produce DA beyond A to E with DE = 90°, and CB beyond B to F with CF = 90°.
- Claim: angle E = 90°, angle F = 90° + CD, and EF = D - 90°.
- Gauss's proof: 'DF is a quadrant, whence everything follows.'
- Expansion (mine): CB is perpendicular to CD at C and CF = 90°, so F is the pole of the great circle CD. Hence DF = 90° and FD is perpendicular to CD.
- Since DE = DF = 90°, D is the pole of the great circle EF. So angle E = 90° and angle DFE = 90°.
- EF equals the angle EDF = ADC - CDF = D - 90°.
- Angle BFE = CFD + DFE = CD + 90°, because the angle at a pole equals the intercepted arc.
- Result: ABFE is again trirectangular, with right angles at E, A, B. Its middle vertex is A, with sides AB and AE = 90° - AD; its opposite sides are EF = D - 90° and BF = 90° - BC; its fourth angle is 90° + CD.
- This is the 'associated quadrilateral' step, essentially Napier's rules and the cyclic chain behind Gauss's pentagramma mirificum.

(4) Set-up for deriving spherical area and trigonometry from additivity of area.
- Notation: R = right angle; rho = quadrant of a great circle; lambda = one eighth of the sphere's area (the area of the octant triangle, whose excess is R).
- F(a,b) is the area of the trirectangular quadrilateral whose middle right angle has adjacent sides a, b. The opposite sides are alpha (opposite a) and beta (opposite b), and the fourth angle is R + omega.
- The figure tiles a larger region with sides rho, rho by copies of this configuration, using theorem (3). The labels are rho - alpha, rho - a, rho - b, rho - beta, the arc rho*omega/R (= EF = D - 90° in arc units), and the angles R + R*alpha/rho and R +/- R*beta/rho (= 90° + CD).
- Definitions: for infinitesimal a, F(a,b) = a*f(b), i.e. a thin strip of width a and length b. For infinitesimal b, f(b) = k*b (Euclidean in the small).

Continuation on p.180 (for orientation; note that transcription's 'ℓ' is beta):
- omega = R*F/lambda (area proportional to excess).
- alpha = (rho/lambda)*F(a, rho - beta), using the associated quadrilateral from (3).
- From additivity, d f(b) = db*(rho*k/lambda)*f(rho - b), so f(b) = (lambda/rho)*sin(rho*k*b/lambda).
- On the unit sphere this is f(b) = sin b, since the strip area is integral_0^b a*cos t dt = a*sin b.

This is a synthetic, analytic derivation of spherical area and trigonometric functions from area additivity. It is of the type one would adapt to non-Euclidean geometry.
errors: Item (2) is false in general. The graph equation (1+q^2)r - 2pqs + (1+p^2)t = 0 is not invariant under conformal maps of the base plane. Only the Laplace equation is invariant. Counterexample: the plane z = x composed with t -> t^2 gives z = Re sqrt(u+iv), whose graph is not minimal. Its level curves are parabolas, and a harmonic graph is minimal only if its level curves are straight. The statement holds only for similarities. Gauss may have confused this with the harmonicity of coordinates in isothermal parameters. The crossed-out 'dritte' (third coordinate) hints at that context.
Item (1) is correct, but only local. f(t/a) + f'(a/t) is a Laurent series valid in an annulus around |t| = a, so the formula characterizes maps of the circle onto itself, not of the disc onto itself.

Theorem (3) is correct. The text does not say that the middle vertex of the new quadrilateral is A rather than B. Applying the quadrilateral formulas with B as middle gives wrong angles. It is fine as stated.

The definitions F(a,b) = a f(b) (to first order in a) and f(b) = k b (to first order in b) are tacit assumptions of differentiability and local Euclidean behaviour. They are not proved, but they are legitimate.

results.what: General form of analytic maps carrying |t| = a onto itself: T = t*exp(i(f(t/a) + conj-coefficient f(a/t)))
results.modern_name: Schwarz reflection principle / symmetric Laurent series for maps preserving a circle
results.usually_credited_to: H. A. Schwarz (reflection principle, 1869-70); conformal mapping theory after Gauss 1822 and Riemann 1851

results.what: Claim that the height of a minimal graph, transplanted by a conformal map of the base plane, is again minimal
results.modern_name: (false) conformal invariance; true only for harmonic functions (Laplace equation)

results.what: Trirectangular spherical quadrilateral ABCD; extending DA and CB to quadrants gives an associated trirectangular quadrilateral ABFE with E = 90°, F = 90° + CD, EF = D - 90°
results.modern_name: Associated (Lambert) quadrilaterals; Napier's rules; chain behind the pentagramma mirificum / Engel-type correspondence
results.usually_credited_to: Napier (1614) for the underlying rules; Gauss for the pentagramma mirificum (Nachlass, Werke III/VIII); Engel and others for the quadrilateral-pentagon correspondences

results.what: Programme to derive the area function F(a,b) of a trirectangular spherical quadrilateral, and hence sin and cos, from area additivity and an infinitesimal-strip ansatz F = a f(b), f(b) ~ k b
results.modern_name: Functional/differential-equation derivation of spherical trigonometry from area (analogue of neutral-geometry approaches that give sinh in the hyperbolic case)
results.usually_credited_to: Generally associated with the foundations of non-Euclidean geometry (Lobachevsky, Bolyai); Gauss's area results are known from his 1832 letter on Bolyai

deep.surprise_reason: The circle-preserving map formula and the spherical associated-quadrilateral theorem are elementary and fit Gauss's known work on conformal mapping and the pentagramma mirificum. The area-from-additivity derivation is a nice unpublished methodological detail with plausible links to his non-Euclidean interests, but its result (f = sin) is classical. The minimal-surface remark is erroneous rather than prescient.

checkable.sympy: a,th=symbols('a th',positive=True); c1,c2=symbols('c1 c2'); t=a*exp(I*th); E=I*(c1*(t/a)+c2*(t/a)**2+conjugate(c1)*(a/t)+conjugate(c2)*(a/t)**2); simplify(re(expand_complex(E)))==0
checkable.asserts: The exponent in T = t*exp(i(f(t/a)+f'(a/t))) is purely imaginary on |t| = a, so |T| = a there
Counterexample to item (2): the plane z = x transplanted by t -> t^2 gives z = Re sqrt(w), which is not a minimal graph
Fourth angle D of a spherical trirectangle with middle sides a, b satisfies cos D = -sin a sin b; opposite sides satisfy tan(beta) = tan(b)cos(a) and sin(alpha) = sin(a)cos(beta)
In the associated quadrilateral (middle sides a and 90°-beta), sin EF = sin a * cos BF = sin a sin b = sin(D-90°), consistent with EF = D - 90°
On the unit sphere F(a,b) = excess = asin(sin a sin b), so for infinitesimal a, F = a f(b) with f(b) = sin b (k = 1, lambda/rho = 1)
Area of a thin trirectangular strip of width a and length b on the unit sphere is a sin b
f(b) = (lambda/rho) sin(rho k b/lambda) solves f'(b) = (rho k/lambda) f(rho-b) when rho^2 k/lambda = pi/2 (unit sphere: rho = lambda = pi/2, k = 1)

transcription_corrections: The insertion above 'Punkt' reads 'der Proj. Ebne' (der Projections-Ebne), an interlinear addition; 'dritte' before 'Höhe' is struck out.
'dies wird gleichfalls an einer Superficies minima sein': the image is more plausibly 'in einer Superficies minima' (struck 'wird' replaced).

Figure labels: bottom-right arc reads 'rho - rho*omega/R' (partly overwritten 'ρβ'); bottom angle 'R + R*alpha/rho' with a '−' beneath (i.e. R ∓); right-side angle 'R ± R*beta/rho'; bottom-left 'rho*omega/R'.

In the definition paragraph, 'dessen mittelsten die Seiten a, b anliegen' should read 'dessen mittelstem [Winkel] die Seiten a, b anliegen'; the opposite sides are alpha, beta (Greek beta; the next-page transcription renders it 'ℓ').
